metadata.target: How does nano-vllm admit a new request and schedule its prefill?
metadata.title: Inside nano-vllm — request lifecycle & prefill scheduling

summary.one_line: A request enters via LLMEngine.add_request, sits in scheduler.waiting until schedule() admits it (probing the prefix cache and allocating KV blocks), then the model_runner forwards it and postprocess hashes the filled blocks for cross-request reuse.
summary.description: nano-vllm is a ~1200-line readable reimplementation of vLLM's core inference loop. This walkthrough traces a single request from arrival to its first decode-able state. It deliberately stops before decode + teardown (summarized in S3) — the prefill path is where PagedAttention's chained-hash prefix cache and chunked-prefill carve actually pay off.

scope.input: How does nano-vllm admit a new request and schedule its prefill?

excluded.reason: Tensor-level model layers — outside the scheduler/cache narrative.
Model loading — orthogonal to the request lifecycle question.

scope.importance_criteria: Weighted toward core_flow + entry_point — the question is about how a request flows, so reading-mode goes to the loop, the policy, and the cache primitives, in that order.

storylines.title: Engine pump — request enqueue & per-tick orchestration

importance_scores.rationale: The entry path every user request takes. Conceptually shallow (it's just a loop), but the framing matters — readers need to see that generate() pumps step() which delegates to scheduler/model/postprocess in fixed order.

storylines.summary: generate() loops add_request to enqueue prompts, then while-loops step() until is_finished. Each step() is exactly one scheduler decision, one forward pass, one postprocess pass.
storylines.mental_model_anchor: Think of LLMEngine as a synchronous, single-threaded heartbeat. generate() is the pump; step() is one beat (decide → compute → record); the scheduler, model_runner, and block_manager are the organs it coordinates. No async, no threads, no callbacks at this layer — the only concurrency is inside model_runner via subprocess workers for tensor parallelism.

purpose.stated: Provide an `LLM` class with the same `generate(prompts, sampling_params)` interface as vLLM, while being readable in ~90 lines.
purpose.evident: Drive a batched inference loop by delegating decision-making to a Scheduler and tensor work to a ModelRunner, with PostProcess as the bookkeeping seam.

architectural_context.system_role: Top-level façade over Scheduler, ModelRunner, and BlockManager. Owns the tokenizer and the per-request lifecycle.

involved_modules.role_in_storyline: Decides who runs each tick; owns waiting/running queues.
Runs the forward pass; samples tokens.
Allocates/frees K/V cache blocks; maintains prefix cache.

architectural_context.data_flow: user → generate → add_request → scheduler.waiting; generate → step → schedule → model_runner.run → postprocess → outputs → user

storylines.change_overview: Two columns. Column 1 (`generate`) holds the enqueue loop and the pump loop. Column 2 (`step`) holds the three sequential phases of one tick. The CALL edge from `generate.PUMP UNTIL DONE` into `step.SCHEDULE` makes the delegation visible.

cols.label: generate
cols.description: Top-level entry point. Pumps the engine by calling add_request for every prompt, then loops step() until the scheduler reports done. Pure orchestration; the heavy lifting happens inside step().

blocks.title: ENQUEUE LOOP
blocks.one_liner: Tokenize every prompt into a Sequence and push onto the scheduler's waiting deque — no GPU work yet, just bookkeeping that the next step() will see.

lines.content: for prompt, sp in zip(prompts, sampling_params):

right_panel.what_it_does: Calls `self.add_request(prompt, sp)` for each input. Inside add_request: if prompt is a string, tokenize via the bundled tokenizer; construct a `Sequence(token_ids, sp)` with `status=WAITING`; call `self.scheduler.add(seq)` which is `self.waiting.append(seq)`.
right_panel.why_its_here: The engine doesn't admit a request until the scheduler picks it up on a future tick. Enqueueing all prompts upfront lets the scheduler batch them; the scheduler then decides who runs and when based on token budget and chunked-prefill rules.
failure_mode: No failure path: the loop body is pure bookkeeping — a tokenizer crash would surface from add_request, not from generate()'s loop.

blocks.title: PUMP UNTIL DONE
blocks.one_liner: `while not is_finished(): self.step()` — the heartbeat. is_finished() is True exactly when both waiting and running queues are empty.

right_panel.what_it_does: A while-loop that calls `self.step()` until `self.is_finished()` returns True. Between calls it records throughput; on each step's return it grabs any completed sequences' `(seq_id, completion_token_ids)` and accumulates them into `outputs`.
right_panel.why_its_here: One step() = one scheduler decision + one model forward pass + one postprocess. The loop drives the engine until both queues drain. Output is collected here because the scheduler returns finished seqs as it removes them from running.
failure_mode: A bug that leaves a seq in WAITING/RUNNING without progress is the canonical livelock here — is_finished() never returns True. Defensive: scheduler.preempt() exists to evict stuck seqs back to waiting under memory pressure.

cols.label: step
cols.description: One tick of the engine. Three sequential phases: schedule (decide who runs), execute (forward pass on the GPU), postprocess (hash blocks, append sampled tokens, retire finished seqs).

blocks.title: SCHEDULE
blocks.one_liner: Ask scheduler which sequences run this tick and whether the batch is prefill or decode. Schedule may admit new waiting seqs or just advance existing running seqs.

lines.content: num_tokens = sum(seq.num_scheduled_tokens for seq in seqs) if is_prefill else -len(seqs)

right_panel.what_it_does: Calls `self.scheduler.schedule()`. Returns `(scheduled_seqs, is_prefill)` — a list of Sequence references and a boolean phase tag. The scheduler tries prefill first; only if no waiting seq can be admitted does it fall through to decode.
right_panel.why_its_here: Separating scheduling from execution lets the engine's per-tick contract stay simple: schedule decides intent, execute realizes it, postprocess records the result. The is_prefill flag tells the forward kernel which code path to use.
failure_mode: If no waiting/running seq can be scheduled (memory pressure on first prefill + no running to preempt), the call asserts via `assert scheduled_seqs` in the decode branch — fail-loud, no silent stalls.

blocks.title: EXECUTE
blocks.one_liner: Forward pass on the model. Returns one sampled token per scheduled seq.

lines.content: num_tokens = sum(seq.num_scheduled_tokens for seq in seqs) if is_prefill else -len(seqs)
outputs = [(seq.seq_id, seq.completion_token_ids) for seq in seqs if seq.is_finished]

right_panel.what_it_does: `self.model_runner.call("run", seqs, is_prefill)`. The ModelRunner gathers each seq's K/V tensors via its block_table, runs the model (prefill = all prompt tokens, decode = one token), and returns sampled token ids. With tensor_parallel_size > 1, this RPC-calls into worker subprocesses.
right_panel.why_its_here: Side-by-side prefill and decode kernels exist because the access pattern differs: prefill computes K/V for many tokens at once and writes them to the cache; decode reads from the cache and computes attention for exactly one new token per seq.
failure_mode: OOM during prefill should not happen here: the scheduler already promised the blocks exist via allocate(). If it does, this is a logic bug in can_allocate, not a runtime fault.

blocks.title: POSTPROCESS
blocks.one_liner: Hash filled blocks into the prefix cache, append the sampled token, retire seqs that hit EOS or max_tokens.

lines.content: num_tokens = sum(seq.num_scheduled_tokens for seq in seqs) if is_prefill else -len(seqs)
outputs = [(seq.seq_id, seq.completion_token_ids) for seq in seqs if seq.is_finished]

right_panel.what_it_does: `self.scheduler.postprocess(seqs, token_ids, is_prefill)`. For each (seq, sampled_token): call `block_manager.hash_blocks(seq)` to chain-hash full blocks into hash_to_block_id; bump `seq.num_cached_tokens`; append the sampled token unless this was a partial chunked prefill that hasn't completed; on EOS or max_tokens, mark FINISHED and `block_manager.deallocate(seq)`.
right_panel.why_its_here: Hashing AFTER the forward pass means we only register prefix entries for blocks whose K/V is actually in GPU memory. The chunked-prefill carve-out keeps the cache consistent: a partially-prefilled block's content isn't yet committed.
failure_mode: If the seq hit FINISHED, deallocate fires; refcount mistakes would cause use-after-free of shared blocks. Mitigated by atomic refcount decrement + free-on-zero in block_manager.deallocate.

key_data_structures.name: hash_to_block_id
key_data_structures.role: prefix cache: chained hash → physical block_id; populated here, consumed by can_allocate next tick

storylines.title: Schedule prefill — admit waiting seqs into the batch

importance_scores.rationale: The most conceptually loaded code in nano-vllm: prefix-cache reuse via chained hashes + chunked-prefill across ticks + ref-counted shared blocks. Everything that makes PagedAttention work happens here.

storylines.summary: Drains waiting deque under token budget. Per seq: probe prefix cache (can_allocate), gate on chunked-prefill rule, install block_table (allocate), schedule this batch's tokens, promote WAITING→RUNNING if fully scheduled.
storylines.mental_model_anchor: Three nested decisions per waiting seq: (1) probe cache to learn how many blocks are already there, (2) decide whether to take a partial bite (chunked prefill) or wait for a clean slot, (3) commit allocation and either fully promote to RUNNING or leave the seq half-done in waiting. The 'commit' shape — peek then conditionally popleft — is what makes the chunked-prefill loop safe across ticks.

purpose.stated: Implement PagedAttention's allocation + prefix-cache reuse + chunked-prefill in a single readable function.
purpose.evident: Decouple cache probing (block_manager.can_allocate), commit (block_manager.allocate), schedule (seq.num_scheduled_tokens), and promotion (status + queue moves) so each can be conditionally skipped without inconsistency.

architectural_context.system_role: Resource-rationing policy: decides who gets to run next tick and how much they get to compute, while keeping the GPU's KV cache reusable across requests with overlapping prefixes.

involved_modules.role_in_storyline: Owns the policy: who, when, how much.
Provides the mechanism: cache probe + allocation + refcount.

architectural_context.data_flow: waiting.peek → can_allocate → chunked gate → allocate → set num_scheduled_tokens → promote (or leave) → scheduled_seqs.append

storylines.change_overview: Three columns. The main one is schedule() (8 blocks for the prefill loop body). Two helper columns: can_allocate (1 block, the chained-hash walk) and allocate (1 block, the two-stage install). CALL edges from schedule's PROBE CACHE block into can_allocate, and from COMMIT ALLOCATION into allocate, make the helper dispatch visible.

cols.label: schedule
cols.description: Drains the waiting deque while batch has token budget. For each candidate: probe the prefix cache, decide allocation, schedule tokens for this tick, promote WAITING→RUNNING when fully scheduled.

blocks.title: BATCH GATE
blocks.one_liner: Loop entry. Continue while there are queued seqs AND batch hasn't hit max_num_seqs.

right_panel.what_it_does: `while self.waiting and len(scheduled_seqs) < self.max_num_seqs`. Two AND-ed conditions; either failing exits the prefill loop and lets the function fall through to decode.
right_panel.why_its_here: Capping per-batch seq count keeps kernel launch overhead bounded. max_num_seqs is a config knob distinct from max_num_batched_tokens (the latter caps total tokens forwarded; the former caps how many independent sequences share that batch).
failure_mode: If max_num_seqs is misconfigured to 0, this never enters; the function falls straight through to decode. No assertion catches that — would manifest as 'requests never start'.

blocks.title: PEEK + BUDGET
blocks.one_liner: Peek the oldest waiting seq (no commit). Compute remaining per-step token budget; bail if 0.

right_panel.what_it_does: `seq = self.waiting[0]` (peek, not pop). `remaining = self.max_num_batched_tokens - num_batched_tokens`. If remaining == 0, break.
right_panel.why_its_here: The commit (popleft) is deferred to a later block because allocation may fail or chunked-prefill may want to leave the seq in place. The budget is computed fresh each iteration since prior iterations may have consumed it.
failure_mode: No failure path. The break is a clean exit when the batch is saturated.
invariants: After this block, `seq` is a valid Sequence reference and `remaining > 0`.

blocks.title: PROBE CACHE
blocks.one_liner: For a new seq, ask block_manager.can_allocate how many of its blocks already exist in the prefix cache. -1 means the pool can't fit even after counting cached blocks; bail.

lines.content: if remaining < num_tokens and scheduled_seqs:  # only allow chunked prefill for the first seq

right_panel.what_it_does: If `seq.block_table` is empty (new seq), call `block_manager.can_allocate(seq)`. This walks seq.num_blocks-1 logical blocks, chain-hashing each and looking up in hash_to_block_id; returns num_cached_blocks ≥ 0 or -1 if the pool is too full. Compute num_tokens = seq.num_tokens - num_cached_blocks * block_size. If seq already has a block_table (resumed chunked prefill), num_tokens = seq.num_tokens - seq.num_cached_tokens.
right_panel.why_its_here: Probing BEFORE committing the popleft lets us bail without dirtying the queue. The -1 sentinel is checked here so the loop exits gracefully under memory pressure rather than partially admitting a seq we can't allocate.
failure_mode: can_allocate returning -1 here is the gate against silent OOM later. If this check were skipped, the subsequent allocate() would popleft from free_block_ids until it underflowed.

blocks.title: CHUNKED-PREFILL GATE
blocks.one_liner: If remaining < what this seq needs AND batch already has another seq, defer. The first seq in a batch is allowed to be chunked; subsequent seqs aren't.

lines.content: if remaining < num_tokens and scheduled_seqs:  # only allow chunked prefill for the first seq

right_panel.what_it_does: `if remaining < num_tokens and scheduled_seqs: break`. Permits partial-prefill ONLY when this is the first seq in the batch (scheduled_seqs is empty). Otherwise break — leave seq in waiting for next step.
right_panel.why_its_here: Chunked prefill carves a giant prompt across multiple ticks so it doesn't monopolize one batch. But mixing a chunked prefill with another seq's prefill is forbidden — keeps batches homogeneous and the kernel paths simple.
failure_mode: If the AND were OR-ed, a single small remaining budget would deadlock the first seq of every batch.

blocks.title: COMMIT ALLOCATION
blocks.one_liner: If seq has no block_table yet, call block_manager.allocate to install one — refcount-bump cached blocks, popleft fresh blocks for the rest.

lines.content: if remaining < num_tokens and scheduled_seqs:  # only allow chunked prefill for the first seq

right_panel.what_it_does: `if not seq.block_table: self.block_manager.allocate(seq, num_cached_blocks)`. Idempotent on resumed chunked prefill seqs (their block_table is already installed). Inside allocate: for cached blocks, refcount++; for the rest, popleft from free_block_ids and append to seq.block_table.
right_panel.why_its_here: This is the commit point. After this, the seq has GPU memory reserved and the forward pass can fetch K/V via block_table. The idempotency guard matters because chunked prefill re-enters this loop body across ticks for the same seq.
failure_mode: The assert in allocate (`assert not seq.block_table`) is the safety net against double-allocation. If the if-guard were lost, this assert would fire.

blocks.title: SCHEDULE TOKENS
blocks.one_liner: Commit how many of this seq's tokens this batch will compute KV for — capped at remaining budget. Accumulate into the running batch counter.

right_panel.what_it_does: `seq.num_scheduled_tokens = min(num_tokens, remaining); num_batched_tokens += seq.num_scheduled_tokens`. The min is where the chunked-prefill carve actually happens — only the first seq's remaining < num_tokens case triggers it.
right_panel.why_its_here: Scheduling and allocating are decoupled because a seq may be scheduled-but-not-fully-promoted (chunked prefill mid-stream). num_scheduled_tokens tells the forward kernel how many slots to compute; num_cached_tokens tracks cumulative progress across ticks.
failure_mode: If `num_tokens > remaining` and this is the first seq, the seq gets partial schedule and stays in waiting for next tick — handled by the next block's promote check.

blocks.title: PROMOTE OR LEAVE
blocks.one_liner: If all of seq's tokens are now scheduled (cached + this batch == total), transition WAITING→RUNNING and commit the popleft. Otherwise leave seq in waiting for next step.

right_panel.what_it_does: `if seq.num_cached_tokens + seq.num_scheduled_tokens == seq.num_tokens: seq.status = RUNNING; self.waiting.popleft(); self.running.append(seq)`. The popleft here is the matching commit to the L31 peek.
right_panel.why_its_here: The popleft is conditional on the seq being fully scheduled in this batch — partial chunked-prefill seqs stay in waiting and are re-peeked next tick. Status flip is the public signal to the rest of the engine that this seq is now actively running.
failure_mode: A skip of the popleft would leave the same seq at waiting[0] forever; the next iteration's peek would re-pick it, allocate would assert on its existing block_table — fail-loud.
invariants: After this block, if seq promoted: `seq in self.running and seq not in self.waiting and seq.status == RUNNING`.

blocks.title: APPEND TO BATCH
blocks.one_liner: Include seq in this step's return value. Loop back to the BATCH GATE.

right_panel.what_it_does: `scheduled_seqs.append(seq)`. The local list that schedule() returns to step() as the seqs to forward this tick.
right_panel.why_its_here: The list mirrors the running queue addition above but for THIS tick's batch specifically — running may include seqs from prior ticks that aren't being forwarded this tick.

cols.label: can_allocate
cols.description: Walks a seq's logical blocks computing chained hashes, looks each up in the prefix cache; returns how many cached blocks were found, or -1 if the pool can't fit the remainder.

blocks.title: CHAINED HASH WALK
blocks.one_liner: For each block before the last, compute chained hash and look up; first miss terminates. Count cached blocks already in use (no new allocation needed) vs cached-but-free (still need to reclaim from free_deque).

lines.content: def allocate(self, seq: Sequence, num_cached_blocks: int):

right_panel.what_it_does: Loop `for i in range(seq.num_blocks - 1)`. h = chain_hash(seq.block(i), h). If hash_to_block_id misses OR the cached block's token_ids don't match (collision check), break. Otherwise num_cached_blocks++; if that block is in used_block_ids, num_new_blocks--. Returns -1 if free_block_ids can't fit num_new_blocks, else returns num_cached_blocks.
right_panel.why_its_here: The token_ids collision check defends against hash collisions corrupting cache reuse. The 'in used_block_ids' decrement is the bookkeeping that says 'this cached block is already counted as used; we don't need to pop it from free again'. The loop stops at num_blocks-1 because the last block isn't finalized yet (it gets written in postprocess.hash_blocks).
failure_mode: A hash collision that ALSO matches token_ids byte-for-byte would be a false reuse; mitigated by chaining (collision must match the entire prefix history, not just one block's content).
Returning -1 here is the only path that gracefully refuses prefill under memory pressure.

cols.label: allocate
cols.description: Installs seq.block_table. For each cached block: refcount-bump (or migrate from free→used if it was cached-but-free). For each new block: popleft fresh from free_block_ids.

blocks.title: INSTALL BLOCK_TABLE
blocks.one_liner: Walk num_cached_blocks first (refcount or migrate), then walk remainder (popleft fresh). Set num_cached_tokens to num_cached_blocks * block_size.

lines.content: def allocate(self, seq: Sequence, num_cached_blocks: int):

right_panel.what_it_does: Two loops. (1) for cached blocks: if block_id in used_block_ids, ref_count++; else, set ref_count=1, remove from free_block_ids, add to used_block_ids. Append to seq.block_table. (2) for remaining blocks: append `self._allocate_block()` which popleft-and-resets a fresh block.
right_panel.why_its_here: The two-stage walk handles all three block states cleanly: used-and-cached (refcount), free-and-cached (migrate), fresh (popleft). Cached-but-free is the case that prefix cache revival depends on — the block's content is still valid even though no seq references it.
failure_mode: The leading assert prevents double-allocation. Under prefix cache reuse, ref_count++ on a shared block is the mechanism that makes cross-seq sharing safe (block stays alive until BOTH seqs deallocate).

key_data_structures.name: Sequence.block_table
key_data_structures.role: Logical-block-i → physical-block-id mapping used by the attention kernel.

key_data_structures.name: Block.ref_count
key_data_structures.role: Number of seqs pointing at this block. Block returns to free_block_ids only when this hits 0.

storylines.title: Decode pass & teardown

importance_scores.rationale: Important and conceptually distinct (continuous batching + ref-counted dealloc), but the surface area is smaller and the patterns mirror the prefill path. Promote to full if a reader wants to dig in.

storylines.summary: When schedule's prefill loop admits nothing, the function falls through to a decode loop: pop each running seq, may_append a new block if the next token crosses a block boundary, schedule 1 token, fused-forward all seqs together. On postprocess: append the sampled token; on EOS/max_tokens, FINISHED → block_manager.deallocate walks block_table in reverse, decrementing ref_count and returning blocks to free when ref_count hits 0. Hash entries persist in hash_to_block_id even after free — that's how the prefix cache revives freed blocks for future seqs.
